idiom_name: concrete entry point + documented hook, enforced by abc / __init_subclass__ where needed
implementation_notes: The idea survives but the word non-virtual does not exist: attribute lookup goes through the instance, so a wrapper (def save(self)) is always replaceable by a subclass, and typing.final is checked by type checkers only - it has no runtime effect. What Python does provide is the subclass interface: abc.ABC with @abstractmethod refuses to instantiate a subclass that has not provided its hooks (PEP 3119), super() lets a hook call the default implementation, and __init_subclass__ can validate a subclass's hook contract at class-creation time. Name the hook deliberately (`_read_impl` or `do_*`), keep it out of the documented public API, and state in the docstring that the wrapper - not the hook - is what callers use.
code_sketch:
class Reader(ABC):
    def read(self, stream):            # stable entry point: do not override
        self._check_invariants(stream)
        return self.read_impl(stream)  # the extension point

    @abstractmethod
    def read_impl(self, stream): ...   # subclasses must provide this

    def _check_invariants(self, stream): ...
pitfalls: Nothing stops a subclass from overriding the entry point; typing.final only turns it into a type-checker error, and only for callers that run a checker.
@abstractmethod is enforced at instantiation time, not at class-definition time - an incomplete subclass fails when it is constructed, so tests must actually instantiate it.
Calling a hook from __init__ dispatches before the subclass has initialised its own state.
